target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would broadly solve the voting-time problem for working Americans.
objection: A national holiday would not reliably help low-income voters because federal holiday status does not require private employers to give paid time off. Many retail, service, and other essential workers would still have to work, so the people most likely to lose wages may still face the same limited polling-hour constraint.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday is the best or most reliable reform for improving turnout.
objection: Instead of relying on a holiday, reforms that directly reduce work-related barriers—such as state laws requiring employers to provide time to vote, expanded early voting, vote-by-mail, and automatic voter registration—are more dependable and better targeted to the access problem.

target: AG1’s implication that international practice proves a U.S. Election Day holiday is an effective turnout solution.
objection: The OECD comparison does not show that a U.S. national holiday is the most effective approach, because many other countries vote on weekends or days when normal work and school do not run; that is different from a U.S. holiday that still leaves many private-sector workers on the job.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday creates a broad structural fix for scheduling conflicts.
objection: The holiday’s effect would be uneven because many low-income workers in retail, food service, caregiving, transportation, and other essential jobs would still be working, and a federal holiday does not force private employers to provide paid time to vote, leaving the underlying economic risk intact.

target: AG1’s idea that a holiday is a good complement to other reforms rather than a substitute.
objection: Making Election Day a holiday could crowd out stronger, more enforceable access measures. Because it does not compel private paid leave, it is a weaker tool than state-level voting-time guarantees and reforms that directly reduce the need to miss work.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday substantially changes the voting-day baseline for workers.
objection: Even if some workplaces close or reduce hours, a national holiday still does not guarantee paid time off or protection from lost wages, so the benefits would skew toward workers with more flexible schedules rather than the low-income workers most affected by time and pay constraints.

target: AG1’s argument that political popularity makes a holiday a strong reform.
objection: Being politically achievable is not the same as being effective. If research shows that an election holiday by itself is not a consistently effective turnout strategy, then making it the central reform risks distracting from better, more enforceable access policies.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces scheduling friction because employers would likely shorten hours or close.
objection: A federal holiday does not control private shift assignments. Many service and essential jobs can still operate with partial staffing, so workers may still have to fit voting into the same limited polling window or lose wages, meaning the scheduling barrier remains.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces the need to ask permission or fear retaliation at work.
objection: A national holiday does not prohibit employers from remaining open or penalizing workers who need time off, so the need to request coverage, face possible retaliation, or risk wage loss can still persist for low-wage workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday helps parents and caregivers by easing household logistics.
objection: Even if schools close, low-income parents may still be scheduled to work, and holiday status can also reduce childcare availability or make it more expensive. So the household-logistics benefit is not guaranteed and may not materialize for the families most constrained by work and caregiving.

target: AG1’s view that a holiday should be adopted because it is broadly supported and can be stacked with other reforms.
objection: A holiday may still be a weaker, less enforceable tool than targeted reforms. It does not expand the voting window or guarantee accommodation, so if enacted without stronger worker protections it can leave low-income voters only partially helped while reducing urgency for more effective measures.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday meaningfully lowers the opportunity cost of voting.
objection: Lowering inconvenience is not the same as expanding access. Polls still operate in limited hours, and workers who must work on holidays may still face the same tradeoff of losing wages or asking for time off, so the holiday does not directly fix the mechanisms that block low-income voters.

target: AG1’s argument that a national holiday is a consistent, near-term solution compared with patchwork state rules.
objection: A holiday may increase convenience, but it still leaves Election Day as a single-day, limited-window process. If more people vote on the same day, polling places can become more crowded, causing longer lines and waits that again translate into time off, wage loss, or lost voting opportunities for shift workers.
